query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The ability to obtain a single‐phase noble metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticle is controlled by a narrowly tuned, kinetically limited disorder-to-order transition. During rapid heating, a well‐mixed disordered (HEA) precursor is formed; then, a precisely limited re‐heating period at a temperature near 1100 K initiates just enough atomic diffusion to lower the system’s Gibbs free energy (driving formation of an ordered intermetallic state) without allowing excessive atomic migration that would lead to phase separation or elemental segregation. The balance between diffusion activation barriers (which differ owing to intrinsic mixing enthalpies and vapor pressures of the constituent elements) and the available thermal “reaction time” under rapid cooling is therefore the key mechanistic variable governing the ultimate crystal-structure selection.
generation.material_initial_state: Disordered solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles formed by rapid Joule heating of a noble metal salt precursor mixture (containing >5 elements) resulting in ~5 nm particles.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust the re-heating (hold) time at ~1100 K after the initial rapid heating step. For example, compare a shortened re-heating period (e.g., 2 minutes) and an extended one (e.g., 8 minutes) with the baseline 5-minute protocol.
generation.conditions: Maintain a synthesis temperature around 1100 K; use a rapid heating pulse (~55 ms) to generate the disordered precursor; fix particle size and composition (noble metal based, >5 elements) on a suitable substrate; and ensure rapid cooling (~10^4–10^6 K/s) after the re-heating period.
generation.structural_mediator: The extent of atomic diffusion and local rearrangement during the controlled re-heating step, which mediates the transition from a disordered solid-solution to an ordered, thermodynamically stabilized intermetallic state without initiating large-scale segregation.
generation.mechanism: In the baseline process, the initial rapid heating traps a highly mixed, metastable state. A controlled re-heating period provides just enough thermal energy to allow limited atomic rearrangement that reduces the system’s free energy (favoring an ordered single phase) without enabling significant element-specific mobility. If the re-heating period is too short, the system will remain disordered; if it is too long, differences in activation energies (due to differing mixing enthalpies and saturation vapor pressures) allow certain elements to segregate or form separate phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: At the baseline re-heating time (≈5 minutes), a single-phase ordered MPEI with uniform elemental distribution and nanoscale crystallites will form. Shortening the re-heating time (e.g., to 2 minutes) is predicted to yield incomplete ordering and retain a disordered structure, while extending the re-heating time (e.g., to 8 minutes) is predicted to result in signs of phase separation, elemental segregation, and possibly uncontrolled particle growth.
generation.baseline: Single-phase, ~5 nm noble metal HEA nanoparticles synthesized via an initial rapid heating (~55 ms at ~1100 K), followed by a 5-minute re-heating period and rapid cooling.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies to noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles (with >5 elements) synthesized under rapid thermal regimes (heating on the order of tens of milliseconds, a hold near 1100 K for a few minutes, and cooling rates in the range of 10^4–10^6 K/s). It is expected to break down if the synthesis temperature or hold time is outside the optimal window that restricts atomic mobility (e.g., much higher temperatures or significantly longer hold periods may lead to uncontrolled phase separation or growth).
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the disorder-to-order transition and kinetic trapping ideas discussed in PMC8797181 (demonstration of the re-heating induced disorder–to-order transition) and PMC10873330 (influence of kinetics and nucleation temperature gaps on multicomponent mixing). The extension here is the specific prediction that adjusting the re-heating duration can control the extent of ordering versus segregation. Uncertainties remain regarding the precise activation energy thresholds and how subtle variations in precursor chemistry may influence the diffusion kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of noble metal HEA nanoparticles using the standard rapid Joule heating protocol but vary only the re-heating duration (for example, 2 minutes, 5 minutes, and 8 minutes) while keeping all other synthesis parameters constant. Characterize the resulting nanoparticles using XRD for phase identification, HAADF-STEM for morphology, and EDS mapping for elemental homogeneity.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns to determine whether a single-phase or phase-separated structure is formed
High-resolution (HAADF) STEM imaging for particle morphology and crystallite size
EDS elemental mapping to assess the uniformity of elemental distribution
Thermal analysis to detect onset of decomposition or unwanted growth
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic variation of the re-heating duration does not lead to observable differences in the degree of ordering or elemental segregation (i.e., all samples remain single-phase and uniformly mixed regardless of treatment), then the hypothesis that the kinetics of the disorder-to-order transition govern the crystal structure selection would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. The proposed formation principle is supported by simulations of the nanoparticle formation

To address the above challenge, we propose an ultrafast (<100 ms), one-step method for the continuous synthesis of HEA NPs directly from a mixture of pure elemental metal powders by using a thermal plasma jet. Thermal plasma jets are partially ionized gases with high temperature (>8000 K) and high speed. They are capable of rapid heating of feedstock to produce an atomically mixed multi-component vapor, and also rapid cooling of the vapor at an ultrahigh cooling rate of 105 − 106 K s−1 to form solid-solution particles. Feedstock can be injected continuously, thus this technology is well suited for scalable synthesis of HEA NPs. Despite this unique potential, thermal plasma jets have only been used for the processing of bulk HEAs or spheroidization of pre-alloyed HEA powders. The main challenge would be the existence of a large nucleation temperature gap among different metal vapors; upon plasma jet cooling, the element with the lowest saturation vapor pressure reaches the supersaturated state first and segregates.

In this work, we demonstrate the synthesis of nanoscale MPEIs (4 to 5 nm) that contain up to eight different elements without particle growth or phase separation via a unique multi-elemental disorder-to-order (HEA to MPEI) phase transition strategy (Fig. 1A). Specifically, we first rapidly Joule-heated metal salt precursors on the carbon substrate [x-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy characterization in fig. S2] at ~1100 K for 55 ms to produce disordered solid-solution HEA nanoparticles as the starting material (). We then use the precise heating control made possible by this Joule-heating approach (in which the reaction temperature is controlled by an electric current) to reheat the HEA nanoparticles for just 5 min at ~1100 K to promote atomic rearrangement to a more thermodynamically stable MPEI configuration (i.e., a disorder-to-order transition), followed by rapid cooling to lock the final ordered structure in place. The resulting MPEI nanoparticles feature an intermetallic structure that has two sublattices (A1B1) (fig. S3a). The temperature profile and structural evolution of nanoparticles over time are illustrated in Fig. 2A. We first synthesize solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles () by heating the metal precursors for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K. This is a critical step for mixing the different elements without phase separation. A disorder-to-order phase transition is then achieved by rapidly reheating the materials to ~1100 K for an additional ~5 min—a limited amount of time that is sufficient to complete the desired transition from the disordered HEA structure to the ordered, single-phase MPEI configuration while simultaneously avoiding nanoparticle growth/agglomeration. Last, the single-phase MPEI structure and small particle size (~5 nm) is preserved by rapidly cooling the materials (~104 K/s).
